title: Pickle deserialization ({lang})
description: Python code reconstructs objects from pickle bytes with {sink}. Pickle runs callables recorded in the byte stream while loading, so bytes from an untrusted source can execute code. This lexical rule flags the load; the reviewer confirms the source is trusted or switches to {safe}.
remediation: Replace pickle with {safe}. If pickle must remain for internal state, authenticate the bytes with an HMAC key and verify it before loading.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the pickle load call regardless of where the bytes came from.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on pickle load calls in Python code.
fp: Pickles written and read by the same trusted process are the common false positive.
recordDesc: Python pickle loads execute callables named in the byte stream, so bytes from an attacker are code execution. The remedy is {safe}.
applicability: Python code that loads pickle data from files, caches, queues, or network sources; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Remote code execution when untrusted bytes reach a pickle load; HIGH severity.
why: Python pickle loads run code embedded in the byte stream ({sink}).
fix: Switch the format to {safe} with explicit field mapping.
If pickle is required for internal state, authenticate the bytes with an HMAC before loading.
verifyT: Rescan shows no pickle load on untrusted input.

python:pickle: JSON or a typed schema with validation

title: PyYAML load without a safe loader ({lang})
description: Code in {lang} calls yaml.load without a Loader argument. The default loader can construct arbitrary Python objects from tags, so untrusted YAML can execute code. This lexical rule flags the call; the reviewer confirms trust or uses {safe}.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: flags any yaml.load call on a line with no Loader= argument. Loader= set on a later line is not seen.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on yaml.load calls without a Loader argument.
fp: Trusted, build-time configuration files are the common false positive.
recordDesc: PyYAML yaml.load without a safe loader can build arbitrary objects from YAML tags. Untrusted YAML can run code. The remedy is {safe}.
applicability: Python code parsing YAML from files, requests, or stored data; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Code execution from attacker-supplied YAML; HIGH severity.
why: PyYAML yaml.load without a safe loader builds arbitrary Python objects.
fix: Use {safe} for untrusted YAML.
Pass Loader=SafeLoader explicitly when yaml.load is kept.
verifyT: Rescan shows every yaml.load on untrusted input names a safe loader.

title: XMLDecoder object deserialization ({lang})
description: Java code builds an XMLDecoder with {sink}. XMLDecoder instantiates objects and invokes methods named in the XML document, so untrusted XML reaches code execution. This lexical rule flags the construction; the reviewer confirms trust or switches to {safe}.
remediation: Replace XMLDecoder with {safe}. Never feed XMLDecoder data that an external party controls.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the constructor regardless of the input source.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on XMLDecoder construction in Java code.
fp: XMLDecoder reading files the application wrote itself is the common false positive.
recordDesc: XMLDecoder turns XML elements into object construction and method calls. Attacker-controlled XML is a known code execution route. The remedy is {safe}.
applicability: Java code that decodes XML documents from files, requests, or stored data; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Remote code execution when untrusted XML reaches XMLDecoder; HIGH severity.
why: XMLDecoder builds objects and calls methods from XML, so untrusted XML runs code ({sink}).
fix: Parse data with {safe} against a fixed schema.
Keep XMLDecoder only for trusted, application-written files.
verifyT: Rescan shows no XMLDecoder on untrusted input.

title: Expression parsing ({lang})
description: Java code parses an expression string with {sink}. Spring Expression Language evaluates method calls and property access, so an expression built from untrusted input can run code on the server. This lexical rule flags the parse call; the reviewer confirms the string is fixed or uses {safe}.
remediation: Parse only fixed expressions. Evaluate user-influenced data through {safe} and keep user input out of the expression text.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the parse call regardless of where the string came from.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on expression-parser calls in Java code.
fp: Fixed expressions defined in code are the common false positive.
recordDesc: An expression language evaluates code-like syntax. If user input becomes expression text, the attacker writes the expression. The remedy is {safe}.
applicability: Java code that evaluates expressions in Spring or other EL-based frameworks; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Code execution on the server when untrusted text becomes an expression; HIGH severity.
why: Expression text built from input is evaluated as code ({sink}).
fix: Keep expression text constant and pass user data as variables through {safe}.
Use a SimpleEvaluationContext to restrict reachable methods when expressions are dynamic.
verifyT: Rescan shows no parse call whose text comes from untrusted input.

java:spring: a fixed expression with variables bound through SimpleEvaluationContext

cweDef.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an Expression Language Statement ('Expression Language Injection')
cweDef.summary: When user text becomes part of an expression evaluated by a framework, the attacker writes code-like syntax that the framework executes.

title: Shared static SimpleDateFormat ({lang})
description: A Java class keeps a SimpleDateFormat in a static field. SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe, so concurrent requests that format or parse through the shared instance can corrupt each other's data. This lexical rule flags the static field; the reviewer moves the formatter to {safe}.
remediation: Create a formatter per call, or wrap one in a ThreadLocal, or use java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter, which is immutable.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: flags a static SimpleDateFormat field regardless of whether it is ever shared across threads.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on static SimpleDateFormat fields in Java code.
fp: Single-threaded tools and batch jobs are the common false positive.
recordDesc: A shared SimpleDateFormat mutates internal state during formatting and parsing. Concurrent use yields wrong dates or exceptions. The remedy is {safe}.
applicability: Java servlets, services, and components holding formatter fields; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Corrupted timestamps and cross-request data mix-ups under concurrency; LOW severity.
why: A static SimpleDateFormat field is shared by every thread that uses the class.
fix: Use java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter, which is immutable and thread-safe.
Create the SimpleDateFormat inside each method call.
verifyT: Rescan shows no static mutable formatter field.

java:text: private static final SimpleDateFormat FMT = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd");
private static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> FMT = ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"));

cweDef.name: Unsynchronized Access to Shared Data in a Multithreaded Context
cweDef.summary: Shared static state accessed by concurrent threads without synchronization can be corrupted, leaking data between requests.

title: WebView JavaScript bridge ({lang})
description: Android code in {lang} exposes a Java object to web content with {sink}. Any page loaded in that WebView can call the exposed methods, so content from a remote origin can reach native code. This lexical rule flags the registration; the reviewer confirms the WebView only loads trusted content or switches to {safe}.
remediation: Remove the bridge, or expose only @JavascriptInterface methods on a reviewed allowlist to WebViews that load first-party content.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the registration call. Whether the WebView loads remote content is not analysed.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on addJavascriptInterface calls in Android code.
fp: WebViews that only load bundled first-party assets are the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, addJavascriptInterface gives web content a path into native Java objects. Untrusted page content can call every exposed method. The remedy is {safe}.
applicability: Android apps using WebView; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Native method invocation from attacker-controlled web content on older Android versions; HIGH severity.
why: Exposed Java objects are reachable from every page the WebView loads ({sink}).
fix: Expose only the narrow methods a page needs, through {safe}.
Load only trusted origins into WebViews that expose a bridge.
verifyT: Rescan shows no bridge on a WebView that loads remote content.

title: Unchecked size multiplication in malloc ({lang})
description: C code computes an allocation size by multiplying two runtime values inside malloc. If the product wraps around, malloc returns a short buffer and later writes overrun it. This lexical rule flags the multiplication; the reviewer confirms the operands are bounded or switches to {safe}.
remediation: Check the multiplication before allocating, or use calloc(count, size), which checks the product itself.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: flags any multiplication of identifiers inside malloc. Bounds established on earlier lines are not seen.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on malloc arguments that multiply identifiers.
fp: Compile-time constant sizes and operands bounded on earlier lines are common false positives.
recordDesc: Allocation sizes computed by multiplication can wrap, so the allocated buffer is smaller than the code expects. The remedy is {safe}.
applicability: C code allocating memory from computed sizes; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Heap buffer overflow after an undersized allocation; MEDIUM severity.
why: A multiplied allocation size can overflow and return a buffer that is too small.
fix: Use calloc(count, size), which checks the multiplication.
Reject operands whose product exceeds SIZE_MAX / size before calling malloc.
verifyT: Rescan shows no unchecked multiplication inside malloc on untrusted sizes.

c:libc: calloc(count, size) or a checked product

title: Default Go HTTP server without timeouts ({lang})
description: Go code starts a server with {sink}. The package-level function uses a default http.Server with no read, write, or header timeouts, so slow clients can hold connections open indefinitely. This lexical rule flags the call; the reviewer switches to {safe}.
remediation: Create an http.Server with ReadHeaderTimeout, ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, and IdleTimeout set, then call its ListenAndServe method.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the package-level call. A server configured on a separate line is not recognised.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the package-level ListenAndServe calls in Go code.
fp: Internal services behind a proxy that enforces timeouts are the common false positive.
recordDesc: The package-level ListenAndServe uses a server without timeouts. Slowloris-style clients can exhaust connections. The remedy is {safe}.
applicability: Go services that start an HTTP listener; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Connection exhaustion from slow or idle clients; MEDIUM severity.
why: The package-level call creates a server without timeouts ({sink}).
fix: Build a server with {safe} and call its ListenAndServe method.
verifyT: Rescan shows no package-level listener in production code.

go:net-http: an http.Server with ReadHeaderTimeout and ReadTimeout set

title: Regular expression built from a non-literal ({lang})
description: Code in {lang} constructs a RegExp from a runtime value. Attacker-chosen patterns can contain nested quantifiers that backtrack exponentially, so one request can occupy the event loop. This lexical rule flags the construction; the reviewer confirms the source is fixed or switches to {safe}.
remediation: Use a literal regular expression, or select from a vetted pattern table, or run user patterns through a linear-time engine such as RE2.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: flags any non-literal RegExp argument. Whether the value is attacker-controlled is not analysed.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on RegExp constructors with a non-literal first argument.
fp: Patterns assembled from constants inside the module are the common false positive.
recordDesc: A RegExp built from input inherits the input complexity. Backtracking on crafted patterns is a denial-of-service route. The remedy is {safe}.
applicability: JavaScript and TypeScript code building regular expressions at runtime; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Event-loop blocking from catastrophic backtracking; MEDIUM severity.
why: A RegExp constructed from runtime text can carry a pattern that backtracks exponentially.
fix: Use a fixed regex literal and validate input against it.
Run user-supplied patterns through a linear-time engine such as RE2.
verifyT: Rescan shows no RegExp built from untrusted text.

javascript:regexp: a literal regex or a vetted pattern table

cweDef.name: Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity
cweDef.summary: A regular expression with exponential worst-case backtracking lets crafted input consume CPU. Patterns built from untrusted text are the usual route.

title: Regular expression compiled from a non-literal ({lang})
description: Code in {lang} passes a runtime value to re.compile or a related re function. Attacker-chosen patterns can backtrack exponentially and tie up a worker. This lexical rule flags the call; the reviewer confirms the pattern is fixed or switches to {safe}.
remediation: Use a raw string literal, or select from a vetted pattern table, or use the regex module with a timeout where patterns must be dynamic.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: flags any non-literal first argument. Trusted variables are flagged as well.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on re function calls whose first argument is not a string literal.
fp: Patterns held in trusted module-level constants are the common false positive.
recordDesc: Python regular expressions backtrack on crafted patterns. A pattern from input can exhaust CPU. The remedy is {safe}.
applicability: Python code building regular expressions at runtime; single-line lexical scope.
risk: CPU exhaustion from catastrophic backtracking; MEDIUM severity.
why: A pattern compiled from runtime text can backtrack exponentially.
fix: Use a raw string literal for patterns that must be fixed.
Reject user patterns, or bound them with a timeout-capable engine.
verifyT: Rescan shows no re function fed from untrusted text.

python:re: a raw string literal or a vetted pattern table

title: Ordinary equality on a signature or MAC ({lang})
description: Code in {lang} compares a signature, digest, or HMAC with ordinary equality. Ordinary comparison returns at the first differing byte, so response timing can reveal how much of the expected value matched. This lexical rule flags the comparison; the reviewer switches to {safe}.
remediation: Compare authentication values with a constant-time function such as the one named in the safe alternative.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches identifiers containing signature, digest, or hmac. It does not prove the value is secret or that timing is observable.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on equality tests against signature, digest, or HMAC identifiers.
fp: Public checksums and content hashes compared for integrity are the common false positive.
recordDesc: Ordinary comparison of a MAC or signature leaks timing information about the expected value. The remedy is {safe}.
applicability: {lang} code verifying signatures, digests, or HMACs; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Byte-by-byte forgery of authentication tags through timing measurements; MEDIUM severity.
why: Ordinary equality on a MAC returns early and leaks how much of it matched.
fix: Compare with {safe}.
Verify the MAC over the exact bytes before any parsing.
verifyT: Rescan shows no ordinary equality on signature or MAC identifiers.

cweDef.name: Observable Timing Discrepancy
cweDef.summary: Ordinary comparison of secrets or MACs returns at the first differing byte, which leaks timing to a remote observer. Constant-time comparison closes the channel.
